specPoints.text: understand the roles of oestrogen and testosterone in the development of secondary sexual characteristics

primer.text: Puberty rewires a body in a few years, and the foreman on that building site is a single hormone per sex. This note assigns the changes to their hormones — oestrogen driving the female set, testosterone the male set — and explains which changes both sexes share and why emotions run high while the hormones climb.

lessons.title: Hormones Behind the Changes of Puberty
lessons.opening: Secondary sexual characteristics are the changes that appear during puberty, switched on by hormones: oestrogen builds the female pattern while testosterone builds the male pattern, and both hormones rise high enough to stir emotional changes too.
keyPoints: Secondary sexual characteristics are the body changes that puberty brings.
Their development is controlled by hormones released at puberty.
Oestrogen produces the female characteristics, such as breast development and wider hips.
Testosterone produces the male characteristics, such as a breaking voice and developing muscles.
Both sexes grow body hair and sexual organs, and hormones drive emotional changes.

low.restatement: At puberty one hormone per sex switches on the adult body plan: oestrogen for female features, testosterone for male features.
low.analogy: Two builders following two different house plans from the same street of cells.
low.examPointer: Name the hormone with each list of changes — the spec asks for the roles of both.

medium.restatement: The changes are secondary because the reproductive machinery already exists; the hormones enlarge and repurpose it, adding visible markers of sexual maturity and, through their action on the brain, shifts in mood and interest in sex.
medium.analogy: A software update that reveals features the hardware carried all along.
medium.examPointer: Include the shared changes and the emotional ones — lists that stop at breasts and voices drop marks.

check.stem: Which hormone drives the development of female secondary sexual characteristics?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Testosterone drives the male pattern.
Progesterone maintains the uterine lining; it is not the puberty driver.
Insulin manages blood glucose, not puberty.

check.stem: Which change belongs to the testosterone-driven male list?

options.text: The voice breaks and the testes start producing sperm
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Widening hips is an oestrogen-driven female change.
Menstruation is female, under the ovarian hormones.
Breast development is a female characteristic.

check.stem: Which changes appear in both males and females at puberty?

options.text: Both sexes grow the sexual organs and gain body hair
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Hip widening is female-specific.
The voice break is male-specific.
Menstruation is female-only.

check.stem: Why do mood swings and new interest in sex appear during puberty?

options.text: Because the rising hormone levels also affect the brain and emotions
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
School difficulty is not a hormonal cause.

options.text: Because body hair irritates the skin
options.explanation: Irritation does not drive emotional change.
Sleep demand is not the taught cause.

check.stem: A teenager's voice breaks and facial hair appears. Which hormone is responsible, and what broader process is under way?

options.text: Testosterone, as part of male secondary sexual characteristic development
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Oestrogen, as part of the female pattern
options.explanation: The listed changes are male ones.

options.text: Adrenaline, as part of stress response
options.explanation: Adrenaline handles fight-or-flight, not puberty.

options.text: FSH, as part of egg maturation
options.explanation: FSH matures follicles; it is not the voice driver.

check.stem: State the hormone responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics.
check.modelAnswer: Testosterone controls the development of male secondary sexual characteristics.

check.stem: List three female secondary sexual characteristics driven by oestrogen.
check.modelAnswer: Breasts develop, body hair appears, the menstrual cycle starts and the hips widen.

check.stem: Explain why body hair growth cannot be used to decide whether oestrogen or testosterone is acting.
check.modelAnswer: Body hair grows in both sexes during puberty, so it is a shared hormonal change rather than a marker of one sex's hormone.

check.stem: A clinic charts a patient's puberty progress. State one male-only change, one female-only change and one shared change it would record.
check.modelAnswer: A male-only change is a breaking voice, a female-only change is the start of the menstrual cycle, and a shared change is the growth of body hair.

glossary.definition: The body changes that develop during puberty under hormone control.
The female sex hormone that drives female secondary sexual characteristics.
The male sex hormone that drives male secondary sexual characteristics.
The stage of development in which secondary sexual characteristics appear.
